Conversely, for the more constrained Capacitated $k$-Center issue - a subset of CkSwO, - we demonstrate that achieving an analogous parameterized solution when dealing with highway dimension is computationally challenging, falling under the W[1] class, whereas we find it relatively simpler with doubling dimension values. This distinction is the first documented case where a problem exhibits difficulty with highway dimension, yet is manageable with doubling dimension in a particular scenario.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous findings, including a proof from [Guerrini et al., Proc. ISIT'19], that a lower bound on evaluations can be achieved when errors are randomly distributed, even for large error rates. This paper follows up on [Kaltofen et al., Proc. ISSAC'17] by refining those results in two key ways: introducing a new evaluation bound with reduced dependence on system parameters, and incorporating an early termination mechanism to prevent unnecessary computations arising from overestimating the system parameters or the error bound, both of which were concepts introduced in [Cabay, Proc. SYMSAC'71].

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be used to produce highly pure multi-photon Fock states via a scanning technique and may lead to the development of efficient optical logic gates and other quantum communication applications.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the network freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes, whereas the algorithm guarantees that the malicious nodes' involvement will not significantly affect the estimation due to their limited number compared to n. The algorithm runs on n nodes with an unspecified number of layers, and its users have a specified number of signal rounds and processing capabilities, specifically O(log^3(n)/epsilon^3), and it also provides optimal resistance to interference and malfunctioning nodes. Furthermore, the algorithm offers certain safeguards against malfunctioning nodes by providing three distinct levels of security, specifically against a specified number of malicious nodes (up to 10% of total nodes), against a large but unspecified number of malicious nodes (up to n^(1-delta)), and against an unprecedented but still limited number of malicious nodes (up to n^(2-delta) with an expanded but still

We developed and implemented a novel approach for solving the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints in simulations of complex, matter-based scenarios within numerical relativity. Our method, adaptable to diverse coordinate systems, reduces to the standard conformal transverse-traced conformal 3-dimensional metric conformal framework in specific cases such as the Schwarzschild metric. We tested our technique in two distinct scenarios: one with a conformally flat flat spacetime and a conformally flat matter configuration, and a second case involving a conformally flat flat spacetime and a conformally flat matter configuration within a spherical, vacuum environment. We successfully calculated the solutions to the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints in both cases, demonstrating that our method is effective for a range of conformally flat spacetime simulations.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments require precise energy resolution and quality, which necessitated a thorough assessment of the PMTs. Over four years, starting from 2017, a rigorous testing program for nearly 20,000 20-inch PMTs was carried out by the JUNO team. By examining these PMTs and implementing a series of stringent requirements, the experiment's investigators were able to verify the high quality of the selected instruments. This study outlines the thorough testing procedures used, the specifically designed testing unit for large-scale use, and the resulting characteristics of the selected PMTs.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results for long-term forecasting, yet it falls short in addressing dimensional interactions. Our enhancement of the Informer addresses these limitations in multidimensional forecasting through several key approaches. Firstly, we incorporate an adaptive graph neural network to identify dimensional connections often hidden in time series data. Secondly, we incorporate adaptive graph convolutional networks into spatio-temporal prediction models, enabling these models to recognize dimensional interactions. Our empirical evaluations with diverse datasets have revealed that the integration significantly boosts model accuracy by around 10%.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by atmospheric effects, including atmospheric dispersion that limits high-resolution spectral observations. The use of an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector (ADC) eliminates this distortion by ensuring that different wavelengths reach the detector simultaneously. In order to utilize the full potential of the Large Binocular Telescope's second generation instrument, the MUSE, it is crucial to accurately correct for atmospheric dispersion across its field of view. In this research, we calculate the corrected positions of light beams passing through a MUSE microlens under different atmospheric conditions. The calculations are verified using a finite element method that takes into account both the telescope's optical setup and atmospheric fluctuations across the MUSE field of view. The resulting corrections are then applied in a real-time algorithm to remove distortions caused by atmospheric conditions across the entire MUSE field of view. This research incorporates the MUSE instrument parameters to provide a practical solution for on-time utilization of the telescope.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers to combine their strengths, and pairing them with models of varying architectures; 2) utilizing label information to guide the distillation process and enhance its effectiveness. We introduce a two-stage teacher-training process, where first we train each model to maximize agreement with its peers, and then use label information to re-adjust the distillation. Notably, our method can function with teachers and students of distinct architectures, which is a notable contribution. Moreover, our knowledge distillation framework allows us to model a optimal scoring function, and this is demonstrated to outperform training from supervision alone. Experimental outcomes on various datasets - Lidige, Amazon, and Pinterest - show that our method significantly boosts performance and sets a new standard on these benchmarks.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur as well due to its wave-like properties. A detector can therefore look for these low-frequency fluctuations, rather than just its high frequency oscillations, and is not limited to finding frequencies that are easily within its range. In fact, the low-frequency fluctuations will occur at a range of frequencies, and their amplitudes will vary accordingly, making this technique highly sensitive and versatile. A range of experiments can be used to detect these low-frequency fluctuations, such as using electrical circuits and capacitors in a range of setups, and particularly with a parallel plate condenser by applying a DC voltage and measuring the resulting current in a range of conditions.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive semi-definite matrix. The positive definiteness of the Toeplitz matrix also determines the sparse and non-sparse nature of the Radon measures. The study further includes numerical examples demonstrating the differences in BPC's solutions for various cutoff frequencies and some intriguing patterns observed.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, preventing further modification and customization. Our work fills this gap with an openly sourced compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, allowing P416 programs to be mapped efficiently and effectively to various hardware platforms. Our compiler backend is tailored for P416 programs and supports programs larger than the inherent limit set by the standard consortium. Our research demonstrates the potential for significant program-sized overhead when using fixed hardware resources, highlighting the need for optimal mapping strategies. Our compiler backend can be used with existing consortium-developed frontend tools.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and assigning one critic network per group, each critic is responsible for generating targeted gradients for the corresponding layer group. Notably, our method allows for both critic networks and the main network to be trained with larger models, resulting in improved performance. We also observed that incorporating our method with existing model-parallel training methods surpasses the results of training with smaller, uniformly divided layer groups. Thorough experiments were conducted across various network architectures, datasets, and problem types, demonstrating the robustness and efficiency of our proposed local critic training method.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this research indicates that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit increased stability when subjected to low levels of dissipation.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we conduct the most comprehensive search to date for this type of scenario using data collected between 1994 and 2005, focusing on two cases with distinct properties: a situation where the decay product propagation distance is limited by the hadronization point, and a scenario where the muon decay length can exceed 500 meters. Our analysis shows that both cases remain plausible based on the accumulated data, with a level of confidence that updates a previous study on this topic, significantly expanding its parameters.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass and charge configuration.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with zero inventory levels in the standard L1 framework. Novel contributions involve addressing the issue of non-differentiable velocities with discrete objects and a bounded domain subject to flowing inflows and outflows. Employing a Lagrangian perspective, we establish that solutions exist and are unique and define a notion of weak solutions. Furthermore, we prove that the flow is continuous with respect to time, and also with respect to the space variable under certain assumptions on the system's coefficients. However, the main challenge is the lack of a link between the Lagrangian and Eulerian perspectives due to the non-differentiable nature of the velocities. This problem is overcome by introducing a new notion of solution that incorporates average velocities instead of precise velocities, which is reminiscent of solutions to certain ordinary and partial differential equations with discontinuous coefficients. Ultimately, we prove the existence and uniqueness of solutions in the optimal transport framework and also through a direct analysis of the initial-value problem. One of the key features of our study is the extension of several solution structures, such as the structure of solutions depending on the properties of the system's coefficients, the link between the Lagrangian and Eulerian perspectives, and the link between the continuous dependence of the

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on the very systems they're protecting, either on the company's local network or directly on the physical devices. The resulting constraint hinders performance, forcing compromise on other crucial factors, such as detection rate or false alarm rate. This paper proposes a new technique, known as EfficientCyber, which utilizes machine learning and evolutionary strategies to optimize AI-based cyberattack detectors, enabling them to run efficiently and effectively on resource-constrained systems. The approach involves developing a lightweight classifier using deep neural networks (DNNs) and optimizing its architecture via an evolutionary strategy to find the best balance between performance and resource usage. A comprehensive evaluation, involving various data sets and configurations, shows that the proposed method outperforms a leading commercial solution, offering improved detection rates and lower false alarms rates, as well as increased processing speed and memory efficiency. The research showcases the potential for AI-powered cyber threat detection, emphasizing the importance of balancing performance and resource requirements in real-world applications.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set actions. We explore infinite groups G exhibiting a Schreier growth gap, such as solvable groups, abelian groups, and polycyclic groups, and explain how this property in G restricts the growth of their subgroups, their homomorphic images, and a wide range of their group actions. Moreover, the article discloses a vast collection of groups that possess a Schreier growth gap. It also identifies the limits of the growth function's linear rate among these groups and provides examples of groups with unique growth functions. Lastly, the article relates the concepts of thin subgroups and emek groups to the phenomenon of Schreier growth gap.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs to move about. However, their gaits can be difficult to identify due to the complex patterns they exhibit. Traditionally, identifying animal gait patterns involved manually inspecting data collected from sensors such as GPS trackers, cameras or pressure pads. This labor-intensive process often resulted in discovering new gait patterns which would then be documented in scientific databases. However, we have developed an innovative approach that uses a more efficient and accurate deep learning algorithm to identify gait patterns. This state-of-the-art approach uses sequences of images to identify gait patterns in a more dynamic and less prone to errors manner. Our tests on a dataset containing images of animals such as the dog, the fox and the bird, have shown that our approach outperforms a baseline model by nearly 10%, with room for further improvements and potential applications in fields such as wildlife conservation and bio-inspiration.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the law of gravity, thus leading to incorrect model development. Utilizing the SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) method, which involves the use of real-world and simulated trajectory measurements, it's illustrated how the assumption that each object is governed by a similar physical law can increase the stability of learned models, although significant discrepancies between predictions and observations persist, primarily due to the intricacies of drag dynamics. This research emphasizes the importance of incorporating prior knowledge into data-driven modeling approaches to better reflect the underlying physics of the problem being investigated.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on particles detectable by their tracks in the inner detector and energy loss measurements in the pixel layers of the detector, thus able to capture particles with lifetimes as short as one nanosecond and masses ranging from 100 GeV to 3 TeV. The study explores the possibilities of long-lived particles in supersymmetric models, considering the production of $R$-hadrons, charginos and staus, with mass limits that extend well beyond previous search findings in various scenarios.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 90-degree hole array on an SOI platform achieved a high Purcell factor of 38.7 for an incident wavelength of 920 nm, and the transmitted signal was significantly reduced to less than 0.01 percent of its initial value. Consequently, a high splittable single-photon tone at 885.05 nm was obtained with a high contrast ratio of 165.8 dB. This research enables the optimization of single-photon sources using efficient hole designs to expedite the development and realization of scalable quantum communication systems.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak, a technique which has been applied to various substances like silicon dioxide, boron oxide, polybutadiene and amorphous germanium. Studies on temperature-dependent boson peaks in silicon dioxide and glycerol have also been conducted. Furthermore, x-ray Brillouin scattering measurements have demonstrated that longitudinal sound wave damping in silicon dioxide and glycerol follows a soft potential model prediction, $\omega^4$, particularly in the low-frequency regime.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle behavior and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. This study proposes a 
semi-numerical technique using differential equations with specific boundaries 
at unique points to solve these complex equations with high accuracy. These 
calculations can be done using numerical methods like sector decomposition and 
are then translated into physical scenarios with a series solution, providing 
precision of at least eight digits. This method has an integrated accuracy 
checker and is shown to work with challenging examples like self-energy and 
vertex integrals and two-loop box integrals.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees across. This feature is particularly noticeable in a Galactic ring structure located between 25 to 30 kilometers per second, and can be further analyzed to reveal details about its shape and features. By applying a mathematical technique called Fourier transformation, researchers have been able to study the pattern of waves and identify a spiral pattern in the far-side arm, which is consistent with a spiral pattern in the near-side arm. This pattern indicates that the far-side arm is a massive structure composed of dense gas and stars, which is estimated to extend from roughly 3 to 8 kiloparsecs from the center of the Galaxy. This far-side arm is observed to be more massive than the near-side arm, and appears to be more compact. Based on the observed patterns, researchers believe that the far-side arm may be approaching a state of stability where its growth is slowing. This new discovery confirms that the far-side arm is a spiral arm and reinforces a model of the Galaxy as a barred wedge-shaped structure.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, which, in conjunction with quality diversity, facilitates the creation of a more extensive and diverse solution set. Ultimately, we establish that different optimization techniques uncover distinct solution sets and each has advantages and disadvantages depending on the optimization problem at hand.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, such as those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating groups of three agents and diverse agent preferences, presents an unsolved challenge in the field. A particular approach to determining stable matches relies on utilizing specific value assessment methods for each agent, which can make finding a stable matching more difficult as groups size increase. Contrasting this, our proposal involves using simple and uniform assessment methods for each agent, which we prove can yield stable matches for any number of additional groups. A key component in supporting this finding involves developing a new diagnosis method that can accurately measure how close a proposed matching is to a stable state.

We've developed a theoretical model for valley Hall effect in 2D materials with both conical and wheel-shaped band structures. Our investigation covers not only bulk properties but also edge states at boundaries. It's found that static strain influences the valley Hall response, despite its absence in the unperturbed model. Both valvelike and wheel-shaped band structures exhibit distinct characteristics in their valley Hall responses. Moreover, the valley Hall conductance exhibits variations in both integer and fractional values. At boundaries, valley-Hall-like edge states can be observed under strain, even in materials with wheel-shaped band structures, provided that the strain satisfies a specific condition. These findings offer new prospects for controlling valley degree of freedom in 2D materials through strain engineering.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the stability of these space transformations. This paper demonstrates that any cloud having a stabilizer with nontrivial action will contain a unique central metric space, such that transformations from the stabilizer all converge to this space, thereby indicating that it is zero distance away from all others within that group. The key proof for this lies within our previously established cloud completeness theorem.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created a reinforcement learning decoder for surface code decryption that surpasses conventional state-of-the-art decoding methods, particularly when dealing with widespread noise patterns.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. It achieves this advantage through processes like quantum entanglement that facilitate information exchange between measurement devices, or by creating highly correlated states in multiparticle systems. In interferometry, this technique improves measurement precision by transferring information between spatially separated entities. Building upon this idea, a new idea proposes using a network of quantum sensors as a quantum metrology tool by linking them together with entangled connections, enabling a single beam to optimize multiple sensors' precision. This approach is applied in a study on gas molecules and shows that by entangling two sensors, the precision of their measurements can be improved beyond what is possible with unlinked sensors, confirming the benefits of quantum metrology in applications such as precision spectroscopy and gravimetry.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A prominent increase in prompt photon spectra at high momentum fractions is observed for hadrons carrying a large fraction of the quark's momentum in Au$+$Au as versus $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This is contrast to the observed suppression in Au$+$Au as versus $p$$+$$p$ collisions for hadrons carrying a small fraction of the quark's momentum. This dual behavior supports the concept of hydrodynamic flow and parton loss mechanisms. Additionally, the study provides the first quantitative examination of parton conversion processes and reveals that a substantial portion of the quark's momentum is transferred to hadrons or other particles in both central and non-central collisions.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This relatively straightforward connectivity arrangement makes the digital-analog method particularly appealing for fermionic quantum simulations.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This robust feature set is generated using the Rich Feature Construction (RFC) algorithm, also known as Bonsai, which comprises a sequence of training epochs. The algorithm is comprised of various building blocks, each producing a more comprehensive feature set that serves as a better starting point for optimization. 

The primary feature construction block utilizes a novel type of knowledge distillation where a Bonsai network is trained to produce richer representations that can be used to initialize a separate model, optimized on a different data distribution. This approach enables the model to handle both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios effectively.

OoD performance was assessed using seven benchmark datasets and compared against OoD methods from multiple categories, including conditionally independently trained networks, adversarially perturbed networks, and weakly- and semi-supervised learning methods. The results indicate that Bonsai outperforms

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes an affordable ferroelectric liquid crystal device. This integrated system has successfully demonstrated the formation of various complex structures, including triangular prisms, cat's eye, and a rabbit ear, among others, in both ballistic and propagating regimes with up to 50% efficiency. This research marks the first instance of achieving the aforementioned results.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, variations, and research objectives. In Section 2, we analyze the connections and differences between our research and multiple related studies. Our supplemenetary material includes a detailed proof of Theorem 3.1 and additional technical evidence.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and device performance across different thicknesses under various beam angles. In CMOS sensors utilizing a high-resistivity Czochralski substrate, a notable enhancement is observed, with the sensitive volume increasing two-fold, subsequently yielding significant gains in detection efficiency and spatial/temporal resolution.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of milliseconds even when it detects extremely faint signals. We have successfully tested FAST in the laboratory, showcasing its capability to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere at a similar pace to existing systems. However, we have also demonstrated that its performance falls short in matching the performance of the current generation of exoplanet detection instruments, primarily due to the limitations of the available reference beam's brightness. A proposed upgrade to the system, with the incorporation of higher-quality reference beams and enhanced real-time processing capabilities, has the potential to surpass the performance of the current exoplanet detection instruments and possibly achieve the required precision for successful high-contrast exoplanet detection.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations are performed, utilizing Monte-Carlo simulations, to showcase the benefits of this model, as evidenced by its similarity to the Hull-White one-factor model's Bermudan swaption prices on Bloomberg, and by its alignment with Bloomberg's constant maturity swap rates.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may set limits similar to those of SHiP in a few years, provided that SHiP's results are published before DUNE's results. If DUNE's results are released before SHiP's, its limits may be significantly worse, potentially up to an order of magnitude, due to the differing timelines of these experiments.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed.  Both estimators work by adjusting the estimated residual variances using only the diagonal entries of the hat matrix, resulting in asymptotic equivalence to previously proposed estimators such as the bias reduced linearization method.  This new approach is demonstrated in a simulation study on real world data from a meta-analysis investigating the heritability of depression, in which the predicted statistical properties are confirmed.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, demonstrating that particle energy is drawn from the fundamental electromagnetic field rather than being a contribution to the gravitational field. This research further explores the connection between particle number definitions based on various coordinate systems, specifically Kretschmann and Riemann, to showcase their relationship. Consequently, while particles may be present in the gravitational field as measured by curvature-based definitions, they do not contribute to its energy due to a lack of entanglement between the gravitational field and the Unruh/Hawking radiation itself.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of J/Psi particles. Notably, models that align with small-x data are shown to yield transverse momentum variations consistent with measured values, especially in cases where rapidity is in the forward direction. Additionally, model consistency with ALICE measurements is found across various centrality levels.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method, built upon existing algorithms such as Chandy-Koo and BCOR, also takes into consideration both system software and hardware constraints. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, a prototype implementation was created and tested across different hardware platforms, including IBM Spectrum Scale and Linux filesystems. Performance metrics such as performance overhead, data recovery speed, and hardware interaction were closely examined. The results show that this proposed algorithm outperforms the traditional Chandy-Koo method by an average of 2 to 8 times, and can also function effectively on hardware platforms that lack support for explicit flush operations.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding predictions from binary-black-hole detections at LIGO and Virgo. Our in-depth analysis was based on a large dataset with approximately 35,000 simulations spanning a broad mass-range and encompassing non-hierarchical configurations. We discovered that the distribution of escape probabilities was better described by a normal distribution after applying a square-root transformation. Furthermore, our results revealed that the average peribronchiation distance was consistently 3 times the semi-major axis of the bound binary, and the residual binding energy was found to be directly proportional to the total binding energy and brochiation distance. Our comprehensive study validated the assumptions and simplifications inherent in the LIGO-Virgo's binary-black-hole detection analysis and highlighted the considerable influence of non-hierarchical configurations on escape probabilities, suggesting a need for more extensive analytical and numerical investigation into such systems.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons does not vary by rapidity but decreases slightly at high transverse momentum levels above 25 GeV/$c$ when compared to lower momentum levels. The study found that suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons is greater than that of J/$\psi$ mesons over the entire examined momentum range.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these alterations is
a complex task, especially since many system areas are involved. To improve the
efficiency of this process, we suggest an analysis framework that can locate
malfunctions automatically. This framework relies on formula-based definitions of
system sections to facilitate fine-grained division among them. Once these
malfunction-causing areas are identified, targeted testing can be performed to
confirm the changes, thereby enhancing the quality of the software system as a
whole.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.13% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.78%. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced interpretability through dimensionality reduction in the latent space and medical feature analysis.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a frequency range of 600-1200 keV from the Cassiopeia A supernova remnant using the INTEGRAL instrument. At a 95% confidence level, we found an overall polarization degree of $0.42 \pm 0.08$% for the synchrotron component and $0.30 \pm 0.03$% for the hadronically dominated component of the INTEGRAL spectrum. By combining our findings with lower frequency radio data, we derived a combined polarization degree of $0.38 \pm 0.03$%. We observed significant variability in the angle of polarization across the remnant, which correlates with the age of the remnant's shock waves. We also used our results to constrain the magnetic field's irregular pattern in the remnant. Furthermore, we estimated the number of accelerated protons or ions as $3.3\times 10^{43}$ per second, assuming a specific scenario.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous due to the diverse possibilities of their composition. As a compact star's density increases, its sound velocity also changes, and this relationship can tell us a great deal about its constitution. There is even the possibility that sound velocity may turn negative at very high densities, signifying a significant phase transition. However, this scenario has never been explored in detail using non-relativistic and semi-relativistic models of dense matter, which often include at most eight fermion species and a single proton and neutron component. Consequently, we have undertaken a thorough investigation of dense matter sound velocities within the non-relativistic and semi-relativistic frameworks, developing general, density-dependent formulas for sound velocity that can be applied to any compact star model. These equations show that at very high densities, sound velocity may turn negative, marking a phase transition to a more stable form of dense matter, which could also resolve the universal relationship between mass and compactness that violates the theorem of mass-radius.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance for equivalent resources. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when rotated makes it more resistant to noise from experimental errors.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular movement such as splashing and atomization, the resulting fluid structures can be intricate and embedded in their surroundings. In this work, we employ a technique called skeletonization to extract the fundamental information needed to represent their geometry. By applying a modified version of a previous approach that efficiently captures the dynamics of multi-component flows with distinct interfaces, we successfully simplify the representation of a periodic liquid jet. This involves propagating a gradient through the structure and simultaneously adjusting its interfaces, ultimately leading to their convergence into the essential framework of the jet's morphology. This framework, which represents the fundamental structure of the jet, is coupled with a quantitative assessment of the interfaces' displacement or volume modification throughout the process, thereby facilitating the reconstruction of the original jet configuration. Furthermore, we evaluate several metrics to classify and differentiate the resulting frameworks. These measures encompass conventional parameters such as branch length distribution following their division into constituent parts, as well as a more advanced representation of the structure known as Topology Morphology Descriptor (TMD), which generates an equivalent representation of the structures by encoding the spatial topology into a concise format.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, as well as validating the results using simulations to analyze the impact of various factors. The outcomes of this study strongly indicate that viral movement on surfaces is statistically certain to occur when the virus exhibits enzymatic activity.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry govern the total pseudo-angular momentum of the system, this momentum is zero. By introducing dopants, researchers find that small amounts of oxygen, usually an isotope of oxygen that's about 5% oxygen-16 and 95% oxygen-128, incorporates into the crystal structure without altering its symmetry. The presence of oxygen results in a new inversion symmetric phase, characterized by a transition to a tetragonal F4/$m$cc structure, where one dimension is approximately 1.01 times the original, with the other two dimensions remaining unchanged. This new phase comes with a new set of phonon behaviors, where the total pseudo-angular momentum becomes proportional to the oxygen concentration. The study, utilizing several sophisticated computer models, discovered that even the tiniest particles can affect a material's phonon behavior as predicted by the time-reversal symmetry principle.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the positioning of individual atomic sublattices generates electric polarization, a concept seemingly unrelated to metals and doped semiconductors. However, our findings reveal that, when the conventional approximation is surpassed, nonadiabatic Born effective charges become well defined in metals within a specific frequency range. We also observe that, unlike in insulators, the summation of nonadiabatic Born effective charges from sublattices in metals does not equal zero but rather correlates directly with the Drude weight. These conclusions were verified through calculations using density functional perturbation theory, as applied to aluminum, and to two doped compounds, electron-doped tin disulfide and strontium titanate.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average free path. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range within molecular fluids. Instead, the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation by Landau and Lifschitz provides a more accurate description within this range. Specifically, our analysis validates their hypothesis that the deterministic part of the equation can predict the statistical properties of turbulence without needing any additional assumptions. Our non-dimensionalization approach of the fluctuating forces also reveals that the quantity $\nu^3/\ell^4$ represents a dimensionless measure of the significance of thermal effects in incompressible fluid turbulence. When thermal effects are negligible, our results recover the classic Kraichnan-Edwards-Wilson statistics. When thermal effects are considered significant, our results show that the magnetic and vorticity structure functions exhibit different scaling behavior compared to the classical case. Furthermore, our analysis reveals an inverse power-law relationship between the Kolmogorov length and the cubic root of the free path. Finally, our results on the magnetic structure functions may have implications for future experiments using low- $\Delta B$ detection methods.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external states cancelling out. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, whose field-theoretical properties and computational models are explored. This contrasts with another phenomenon where a magnetoelectric interaction traps a charge equal to $\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf{B}/e$, resulting from a magnetoelectric interaction-induced charge coupling to a magnetic field, essentially equivalent to a magnetoelectric current pump.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments. This paper focuses on a technique called design mining, utilizing text data from these discussions to gain insight into software design. By collecting and analyzing the discussion history from open-source projects over a lengthy period, this paper reveals how the design structure of a software is constantly adapted through this discussion history, drawing on concepts from concept mapping. The results highlight that design mining can serve as a supplementary means of assessing software design, and that this method is resistant to common biases and errors frequently found in traditional design approaches. Furthermore, this paper demonstrates that design mining enables the identification of design features on various levels, from individual functions to overall architectural frameworks. Lastly, this paper illustrates the practical value of design mining through a real-world example, showcasing its potential uses in guiding software design.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a superfluid/supersolid state.
Gravity emerges from topological defects within the post-inflation virtual "condensate" component.
Consequently, it is anticipated that exotic particles that could explain dark matter will not be detected at the LHC.
Moreover, it is suggested that the de Sitter horizon associated with holographic dark energy acts as a complete absorber for static detectors, given its infinite redshift effect.
As a result, thermal radiation emitted from this future de Sitter horizon may be the source of dark vacuum energy.

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By assuming a proximal gradient method is able to recognize the differentiability manifolds in a nonsmooth objective, we show that incorporating Riemannian Newton-like techniques alongside the proximal gradient steps results in a significantly improved convergence rate for specific nondegenerated nonsmooth nonconvex optimization problems. Moreover, our algorithm is accompanied by a numerical study that includes optimizations regulated by $\ell_1$-norm and trace-norm.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it follows that either the product of $a$ and $b$ is in $I$, or $c$ is in $I$. Our research presents numerous results regarding the characteristics and examples of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. It has been proven that if $I$ is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ where the product of three non-zero ideals is completely contained in $I$, it then holds that either the product of the first two ideals is completely contained in $I$, or the third ideal is completely contained in $I$. Additionally, it is demonstrated that if $I$ is not a $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ but a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal, then $I^3 = 0$. Furthermore, the characteristics of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within principal ideal domains and Dedekind domains have been determined

We present new findings for $B^0$ decays to $K^-$ and $\bar{\nu}_\mu$, as well as $B^+$ decays to $K^0$ and $\nu_\mu$. These conclusions are drawn from a massive dataset collected by the LHCb experiment during a 2011 run, utilizing a proton-proton collision sample with a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV and a total luminosity of 1 inverse femtobarn. The $B^0$ decay to $K^-$ was detected with an almost full reconstruction of the final state, yielding a total branching ratio of approximately 7.7 nanobarns, with the measured mass of the $B^0_s$ particle consistent with established particle physics models. The $B^+$ decay to $K^0$ was optimized using momentum conservation in the detector, resulting in a total branching ratio of around 9.3 nanobarns. These findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of $B$-meson decays and the underlying particle physics that govern them.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies.
