This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of necessary technology, expertise, and
financial resources for sophisticated equipment. While countries like Japan have
introduced more cost-effective and accessible smartphone-based solutions for
automated road condition monitoring, many other countries continue to search for
efficient alternatives. To address these issues, this study contributes in
several key ways. Firstly, it examines the suitability of Japan's approach for
global implementation. Secondly, a substantial, multi-national smartphone-based
dataset consisting of 26,620 images is developed. Thirdly, a set of adaptable
models capable of detecting and classifying road damage in multiple countries is
created, using the proposed dataset. Lastly, guidelines are provided for other
countries to replicate success stories like Japan's, ensuring widespread
applicability and ease of adoption.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation learning becomes even more difficult.  In order to overcome these obstacles, we propose a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert domain.  The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints to ensure that our learning approach doesn't suffer from domain-shift confusion.  Once the domain alignment is achieved, we utilize the aligned trajectories to train our imitation policy.  Ultimately, our framework demonstrates the ability to bridge gaps between disparate domains and achieves high performance on a range of tasks within multiple robotic domains.

A major uncertainty in determining the process behind the formation of the first stars remains unresolved. We have conducted a set of magnetohydrodynamic simulations that involved the collapse of cloud fragments, leading to the formation of protostars. To account for the uncertainties, we obtained statistical outcomes from several simulations with varying initial magnetic field amplification levels and cloud fragment masses. We found that when the magnetic field in the clouds is strongly amplified, secondary protostars form within more massive cloud fragments. These secondary stars have lower formation efficiencies compared to the primary stars and tend to have smaller masses. We found that a very massive cloud fragment (with a mass similar to the total mass of the fragment used in Abel et al. 2002) results in a contracton timescale that is not greatly increased by the magnetic field. This implies that when a cloud fragment collapses to form a second star, it can do so quickly and may lead to a protostar that forms a bit more massive than the second star. We found that when the magnetic field in the clouds is strongly amplified, the mass of the second star contracts more quickly than a neutral cloud fragment, suggesting that when a cloud fragment collapses to form a second star, it can do so quickly and may lead to a protostar that forms a bit more massive than the second star. We found that the mass of second stars formed in our simulations ranges from about 2 to 40 solar masses, depending on the mass of the cloud fragment and

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by parameters such as confidence and support levels. We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Each transaction in a dataset can be viewed as a logical statement, and we investigate existing notions of redundancy among association rules. We explore alternative definitions of redundancy and introduce new characterizations, highlighting relationships between these concepts. We demonstrate that two distinct notions of redundancy exist, differing in how full-confidence implications are treated. We establish a deduction calculus for each of these concepts, show how to create the smallest possible bases, and also examine redundancy with multiple association rules. We fully dissect the case of redundancy involving two partial premises.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This route is optimized using a measure that identifies the most informative locations to collect data from. A novel real-time Bayesian algorithm has been created to constantly update the map estimate and the associated uncertainty metric with every new data point, allowing the process to take place in real-time.

This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering techniques. At its core lies the comparison of sequential data segments. The process involves first mapping these segments to suitable HMM models and then assigning them to categories based on similarity. Anomalies are detected by analyzing the distribution of normalized distances between time series segments and identifying those that deviate from the expected pattern. The performance of this method is demonstrated through classification and regression tasks involving artificial and real-world data sets.

This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modality combination, this investigation extends to exploring the effect of incorporating thermal images on verification robustness. Specifically, state-of-the-art deep learning architectures were applied to establish unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal verification systems which were compared under optimal and impaired conditions. Moreover, a comparison of fusion methods using simple score aggregation and soft attention techniques was also conducted. Experimental results obtained on the SpeakingFaces dataset showed that a multi-aspect verification system outperforms unimodal and bimodal approaches by significant margins under both adverse lighting and noise conditions. Consequently, this work is expected to be a precursor to developing highly robust person verification systems that can function effectively in varied environments and adversarial conditions.

Generating new training data through augmentation is achieved by appending existing examples to create new instances. We've found this approach to be both simple and cost-effective in boosting the performance of pre-optimized Transformer and Conformer models. Specifically, enhancements of up to 2.83 WER and 6.87 WER are seen in the LibriSpeech-960h test sets, and even higher when models were combined with fusion. Moreover, improvements of as much as 0.9 WER are recorded on the CoVoST-2 for several non-English languages following this training methodology. Notably, results indicate the magnitude of gain largely correlates with the size of initial training data. It is observed that our augmentation method can function effectively even when models have not undergone optimization, and it is compatible with models of varying architectures and preprocessing techniques, including those using speech augmentation with Text-To-Speech (TTS) and noise addition. For experimental purposes, a pre-trained model and associated augmented data are made accessible via a GitHub repository.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key research findings include the existence of GMLEs that are robust to the assumptions made about the parameter space $\Omega$ and $\eta(\theta)$, are invariant to any confounding variables, and are consistent when the true parameter space $\Omega$ and $\eta(\theta)$ are known. Moreover, it has been established that the maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs) that assume a parametric form for the distribution of $\theta_i$, denoted as $f_G(x)$, are a specific type of GMLE. This theory is validated through simulations of various scenarios, including a realistic example of estimating the expected value of latitude in a random sample of locations on Earth.

Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework called One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information, as well as demonstrates the creation of an optimization problem for an efficient trade-off between utility and privacy.

In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust emission substructures.
These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations of C$^{18}$O J=2-1 revealed a distinct trough at 88 au that overlapped with the areas of several millimeter dust continuum emission gaps.
However, this gas substructure showed different properties than the dust particles, as it did not follow the pattern of their temperatures or the CO gas column density distribution.
Our models suggest that this gas substructure might be the result of a combination of reduced gas density and elevated temperatures due to photochemistry.
These factors could have caused a drop in the CO column density without affecting the dust particles' temperatures or overall gas density.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced software tool that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an object-oriented approach and a modular architecture, ETA supports a wide range of data processing functions, including basic mathematical operations, real-time plotting, and comprehensive data visualization. By employing an intuitive user interface and a dynamic configuration system, researchers can easily customize analysis settings, compare data scenarios, and publish results. Our comprehensive software package, including ETA and associated utilities, is now accessible through our online repository at https://eta-project.github.io.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring regularity of the cost function, an issue resolved by assuming the cost function meets certain growth requirements. This assumption enables us to demonstrate the existence of an equilibrium with the added requirement of velocity trajectories being relatively bounded.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. Our string structures exhibit distinct spatial patterns, with members either moving in the same direction or scattered across the sky, and their movement trajectories often resemble a zigzag shape. It's also been observed that these structures contain both younger and older stars. Initially assumed to be compact, overlapping entities, our findings indicate that "strings of life" are actually separate individual stars and our analysis of these structures should be reevaluated. Given that these structures consistently appear in clusters, it's possible that they represent specific patterns of star movement rather than physical bonds between groups of stars. These structures consistently appear in clusters, with each cluster composed of 10 to 100 million suns, spanning thousands of light years, and containing similar numbers of stars as our sun's entire orbit. These patterns could be indicative of specific gravitational forces or uneven mass distribution within our galaxy, implying that these structures are actually inherent features of our galaxy's architecture rather than anomalies. Moreover, these structures consistently appear in clusters, with each cluster composed of 10 to 100 million suns, and these strings are generally shorter, containing fewer stars, and are typically found in areas where our sun's orbit meets these clusters. These patterns could imply that these structures are

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive 88% reduction in computational requirements, striking an ideal balance between accuracy and efficiency. We publicly release the VICTOR implementation at https://github.com/stevejpapad/Visual-InCompatibility-Transformer.

The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced quantum physics, enabling the unification of diverse methods to quantify specific quantum effects. It plays a pivotal role in optimizing their utility across various applications. The incorporation of radical quantum phenomena such as coherence, entanglement, and nonclassicality has enabled their application in real-world contexts. The theoretical framework of quantum resource theory categorizes quantum states into 'free' and'resource' sets. Operations associated with free states emerge as compositions of unitary evolutions, and the goal is to discover how to obtain the maximum achievable influence by transforming 'free' states into'resource' states through these operations. Recent breakthroughs have led to the development of powerful methods for achieving this, including the construction of efficient algorithms based on semidefinite programming. The resulting techniques have far-reaching implications, allowing for the precise calculation of the optimal influence when the'resource' set consists of entangled states and allowing for the simultaneous conversion of multiple coherence resources into each other. These advances have led to the discovery of novel methods for converting coherence into entanglement and for achieving optimal tradeoffs between different quantum effects, thereby expanding the scope of efficient resource management in quantum information.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis for FedBuff is developed using the Fomin-Shindin tool and is determined by dependent factors. Empirical testing of FedBuff is conducted on artificial and real-world data sets, demonstrating its convergence rates that are proportional to sqrt(K) or log(K) after stabilization.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude. Primordial black holes with masses in the intermediate range (10^12 to 10^18 grams) might also be responsible for the observed microphysical phenomena such as the observed anomalies in the ${}^{6}\mathrm{K}$ beamline at the LHC and the observed low-energy anomalies in the $\Lambda \mathrm{WMAP}$ data.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we discover that its breaking point depends on the strength of the connections between the particles, as well as how easily these particles move with respect to one another. This finding is consistent with previous research that observed how a floating raft made of particles breaks down when its surface of support suddenly changes size. Moreover, by analyzing the material that breaks off from the raft, we gain insight into the connections between the particles, allowing us to determine the point at which these connections failed, thus controlling how the particles moved back to a more stable configuration. Our observations confirm that three-body interactions play a crucial role in how a particle raft made of soft particles breaks down when its surface of support changes size.

The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility can be enhanced through epitaxial matching of GaN to certain II-IV nitride materials. We performed detailed computations utilizing the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the hole mobility of GaN, revealing that aligning GaN under uniaxial compressive strain by matching it to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ inorganic materials flips the order of the heavy and light hole bands, resulting in a reduced hole mass along the compression axis. Consequently, our calculations indicate that matching GaN to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ boosts its room temperature hole mobility by 50% and 260%, respectively, when compared to strain-free GaN. Furthermore, our model suggests that matching GaN to an fcc lattice of MgSiN$_2$ could flip the order of the valence bands of GaN and InN, making it a suitable material for fabricating p-Np transistors.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly using finite-rank operators even when $P$ is not compact. We also establish that kernel-based techniques outperform traditional parametric methods like Galerkin methods in terms of convergence. Moreover, this research offers a new perspective on the limiting object of nonparametric estimates of $P$. Furthermore, it is shown that these findings are significant for various spectral analysis techniques for Markov transition operators. Our study also provides a novel asymptotic perspective on the kernel conditional mean embedding, which underpins numerous techniques in kernel-based nonparametric inference.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We explore and define the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated properties. We derive recurrence relations, identities and present comparable results for $\lambda$-analogues of Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We also introduce $\lambda$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and provide a formula reminiscent of the Dobinski-like formula.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. In contrast, few existing studies have focused on modifying existing models to consider time frames. This work introduces Time-Agnostic Model Trasformation (TMT), a novel approach to transform static models into temporal models that can accommodate various time frames, including both absolute and relative times. By using TMT to convert existing models, researchers can easily and effectively leverage the knowledge gained from temporal models without requiring extensive knowledge of new techniques. To facilitate this, TMT is implemented as an open-source library, available at https://github.com/asaraht/TMT, where users can find further details and demonstrations of the technique. By using the ConveRation Eval benchmark, an evaluation benchmark for temporal knowledge graph embeddings, experiments show that TMT can successfully improve the performance of existing models. Additionally, the technique is shown to outperform models specifically designed for temporal contexts, and even offers better performance than models that were developed to account for time frames but actually show lower performance.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely hold significant value for ongoing research regarding infinite graphs and their associated C*-algebras. Moreover, this note specifically explores insplits and outsplits as key examples of strong shift equivalences, demonstrating that these equivalences lead to Morita equivalences that maintain consistency across various weighted gauge actions. Consequently, a question is raised about whether strong shift equivalence can be expressed as a product of insplits and outsplits.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between entities.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. Y is derived from a random selection of edges from X, based on the existence of a certain covering map.

Furthermore, we've modified this algorithm to create a more efficient construction, involving a construction of a 3-dimensional expander from a 2-dimensional one, used in the construction of minor closed embeddings in high dimensional expanders and serving as an essential tool for many computational challenges. 

In addition to these contributions, we've established a key concept of 'lifting' and'strengthening' for complexity-theoretic constructions within high dimensional expanders, enabling more robust and efficient constructions, such as implementing minor-closed embeddings and constructing high dimensional geometric graphs that can be precisely mapped to high dimensional expanders. 

We've further demonstrated novel applications and extensions for existing problems, such as constructing high dimensional geometric graphs with local spectral expansion, proving the necessary conditions for constructions like hypergraph matching and constructing large-scale hyper graphs with a certain property called 'hyper-linking'.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements.

We have computed the Benois $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical Artin motives, which aligns with Deligne's framework. The construction proposed by Benois hinges on the selection of a regular submodule. When the representation is $p$-regular, choosing such a submodule is analogous to selecting a'motivic' $p$-refinement, making the process fairly intuitive. However, when the representation is $p$-irregular, things become more intricate as regular submodules are categorized by a flag variety, resulting in an abundance of choices that involve continuous parameters. Despite these complications, our analysis in select examples highlights how Hida theory and eigencurve geometry can facilitate the identification of a limited set of choices that possess notable arithmetic and'mixed-motivic' significance.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully integrated Rydberg atoms with deep learning algorithms, allowing the 
model to leverage the atoms' sensitivity while minimizing the impact of noise 
without requiring the resolution of complex mathematical equations. In a key 
test, our Rydberg-deep learning system has enabled the direct extraction of 
encoded information from frequency-division multiplexed (FDM) signals, marking 
an important breakthrough in this field, and holding the potential to 
revolutionize the sensing and communication capabilities of Rydberg-based MW 
technology.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its parent galaxy's brightness. However, this level of star formation is unlikely to result from the typical, dense gas clouds typically seen in more luminous galaxies like the HII region in UGC 8839. Instead, the extreme off-axis star formation in UGC 8839 might be the result of a supercloud collision or a supercloud losing stability due to a black hole with up to a million times the mass of the sun. These possibilities could provide valuable insights into the processes behind early galaxy evolution.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the oscillating CO$_{2}$ density in the upper Martian atmosphere, spanning between 120 and 190~km in altitude, is monitored. This observation sheds light on the effects of gravity waves (GWs), allowing scientists to analyze the behavior of GWs in the upper atmosphere under isothermal conditions and understand the role that the atmospheric background temperature plays in the propagation of GWs. Data obtained from past missions, including the Mars Global Surveyor, at lower altitudes, is compared to the new findings above 100~km in altitude. The integration of the new data with existing information enables researchers to construct a comprehensive picture of GW behavior in the entire Martian atmosphere.

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions occur when high-energy ions surpass the range of the strong force, enabled by virtual photons exchanged between the nuclei, whose numbers directly correlate with nuclear electric charge. Given its exceptional energy levels, the LHC serves as the most powerful photon source ever constructed, particularly in favouring photoproduction of heavy vector mesons due to their inherent affinity to photons. Recent experiments examining the forward J/psi production in lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions at 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector are featured.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using top-notch graphics processing units can still take several minutes to sample one second of audio. Our approach presents a unified model able to produce high-quality, long-form audio in real-time. We've developed a new, efficient audio model that runs directly on graphics processing units. It generates sound waves with smooth, continuous frequencies by converting visual inputs into musical notes. These notes are then progressed over time using an animation technique. The produced sounds have natural characteristics including pitch variations, volume changes, and the ability to mimic background noise. Our model allows for the instantaneous synthesis of sound when combined with pre-trained audio models. It can also be used in audio extension tasks. These contributions can be immediately played back as high-quality audio.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate gradient flow management. To address these challenges, numerous studies have been conducted. This article aims to provide an overview of recurrent neurons, their variations, and expert tips for efficiently training fully recurrent neural networks, drawing from the Multiple Object Tracking module within our IPO studio software.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel theoretical approach underlying this methodology contributes to the body of econophysics research.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has drawn significant attention. The proposed value method can effectively estimate the impact of each training example, facilitating data selection for refinement or removal. The study of dataset importance has yielded two notable approaches: one based on counterfactual reasoning and the other grounded in Shapley algebra. The latter has been expanded to represent datasets as functions, enabling the calculation of a trained model's value allocation to individual training examples. A notable advantage of this approach is its ability to adapt various learning problem formulations into a uniform mathematical framework, enabling the comparison of different problem formulations. The formulation of a learning problem is understood as a function $f$ mapping datasets to models, and a corresponding task is to find the optimal dataset $D$ consisting of $n$ examples that minimizes the difference between $f(D)$ and a target model or function. The optimal dataset $D$ is shown to consist of examples that follow a specific sequence, and a mathematical formula can be derived to compute the value allocation to each training example. The approach is versatile and can be implemented using proxy surrogates to compute dataset values. The results of experiments conducted on text and image classification tasks demonstrate the efficacy of this approach.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where a required characteristic for the anomalous Hall effect is absent. X-ray diffraction experiments indicate that this phenomenon is not caused by structural changes within the material. The investigation further reveals that when Mn$_3$Sn enters the helical state, its in-plane lattice parameter exhibits unusual temperature dependence, supporting the hypothesis that atom rearrangement significantly affects the material's properties. Ultimately, this research significantly contributes to understanding the interplay between pressure and magnetic ground states in Mn$_3$Sn and its related compounds.

Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to the
domain. Notably, recent studies have established Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) as the
prevalent approach for RE. In particular, the reliability of DNNs in the form of recurrent
neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNN) has been validated
through recent state-of-the-art results. This overview presents a comprehensive review
of the most recent advancements in RE, specifically focusing on the role of DNNs for RE.
Furthermore, our evaluation of the most recent convolutional and recurrent models
shows that a combination of CNNs and RNNs can significantly enhance performance,
with the incorporation of pre-trained word and char embeddings greatly improving
results. Finally, our work addresses future research directions for RE.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task that aims to recover a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that leverages a hypergraph construction model, which is trained and optimized on the basis of certain graph metrics. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate the validity of our theoretical findings and showcase the feasibility of our proposed supervised hypergraph reconstruction approach, which achieves superior outcomes compared to existing unsupervised reconstruction methods.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports necessitates medical
experts to be familiar with both normal anatomy and the detection of anomalies.
Current medical image analysis systems lack the knowledge of anatomical structure
appearance due to difficulty in collecting annotated data, thus restricting their
capability to narrow expertise areas, like diagnosing specific conditions. Our
research addresses this gap by incorporating human anatomy and allowing the
connection between report content and corresponding image content. To utilize
anatomical information, we introduce an advanced system to gather and integrate
human body structures from CT scans and incorporate it into PAXRay. The latter is
a comprehensive dataset comprising comprehensive anatomical information covering
twenty-five years and over three million X-ray images along with associated radiology
reports. Our system enables the integration of anatomical information and enables
the connection between report content and associated image content. This allows
anatomical information to be utilized in a variety of tasks, including as-a-service
visual comparison between human and AI-generated anatomical structures, thus
facilitating comparative analysis between human and AI-generated diagnoses.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, researchers now consider the possibility that this theory could hold for tight contact structures, which are also related to Euler classes of one. To test this idea, recent findings show that previously found counterexamples are also related to tight contact structures, leaving room for the possibility that this theory might be correct for tight contact structures.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Furthermore, we develop a straightforward approach to calculate entropy for any given function. Our study with a microcavity emitting a logarithmically symmetric pattern reveals that as the degree of unidirectionality increases, both the entropy and a commonly used measure of this factor decrease, although the rate of decrease differs significantly. Notably, the entropy-based indicator offers more sensitive assessment of this factor.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model when considering stable relationships with comparators' daily returns, thereby not refuting the efficient market hypothesis.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we reveal its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed Fredholm determinant framework, we arrive at exact solutions that depend on the specific initial conditions of the KPZ equation, allowing for further generalization to other initial conditions.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These measurements are then applied to various solar wind plasma intervals. One such interval is scrutinized, yielding valuable insights into its power spectral density fluctuations spanning from the inertial to sub-ion range. Two possible explanations for these density patterns exist, suggesting that they arise from specific wave types and turbulence processes. A review of relevant research is also conducted, discussing prior studies on the subject. These studies have diverse origins, including Earth-based observations and simulations. The findings from this research are then contextualized within existing scientific knowledge on the topic.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to determine if
two electoral districts are treatable, meaning their election outcomes can be
altered by redistributing voters between them. Our findings indicate that these
two approaches can distinguish between genuine and artificially created districts
at an high confidence level in the US, without exception. Notably, our research
presents the first demonstration of gerrymandering's analytical detectability in
a real-world scenario in gerrymandering's history. Furthermore, our studies show
that a variation of our algorithm can successfully identify manipulation in a
large number of artificial districts, and additionally, that the gerrymandering
probability in the US is substantial. Finally, our research highlights that the
mid-decade census population data employed in the US can facilitate effective
district boundary manipulation by our methods.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. A nonconvex surrogate function and an alternative direction method of multipliers (ADMM) are utilized to improve the low-rank decomposition efficiency and computational speed. Ultimately, the sparse matrix-derived saliency map is segmented to pinpoint defect regions. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques and successfully detects fabric defects.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions on the scene before taking them, which guides its navigation towards the target. Evaluations demonstrate that the agent's augmented policy surpasses a range of state-of-the-art models in diverse target-driven visual navigation tasks, with a significant margin of performance improvement observed on the AI2-Thor simulator.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity within a finite time. In this paper, such constraints are established for general relativity and certain modified gravity theories. It's found that such constraints are strict limits in most cases, exceeding the corresponding limits in linearized gravity. In some instances, such constraints are less restrictive than those in linearized gravity. Furthermore, such requirements are less demanding than Dyson's maximum luminosity limit, which states that the Bondi mass must decrease at least twice as quickly than in a radially inflating three-dimensional spherical space. In addition, this paper explores the associated energy conditions and the related stability of the spacetime, analyzing their interconnections with the mass aspect stability. A simple model is used to illustrate a situation in which the mass aspect undergoes cyclic changes. Lastly, a lower limit is derived for the amount of emitted energy required to remove an amount of Bondi mass.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive black holes formed in the early universe have masses of 10^3 to 10^6 solar masses, influenced by the initial distribution of binary systems and their mutual separation at the formation of the universe's structure.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that uses historical data and real-time measurements to identify potential incidents. Furthermore, this method is designed to detect incidents in real-time and is fully automatic. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on different types of distribution networks and incidents.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly driven by the $\omega$ meson. On the other hand, the cascade decays involving the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are substantially suppressed compared to other diagrams, specifically those that go through the $\psi(2S)$ or a three-body decay of $\rho$ directly into $J/\psi \pi \gamma$. The measured branching ratios for $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ are potentially within reach for the BESIII and LHCb Collaborations. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi\pi^+\pi^- \gamma$ decays may be used to determine the couplings $g_{X\psi\omega}$ and $g_{X\psi\rho}$, respectively, which would offer insight into the isoscalar and isovector components of the X(3872) wave function.

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

The study on varying electron spin orientation employs the coordinate transformation method. Characteristically, Topological Insulators exhibit an uneven spin orientation shift within the Brillouin zone. By mapping Topological Insulators with a Topological Charge defect, we find that their surface energy spectra develop discrete energy gaps consistent with the lattice dislocation density. These defects create non-topological surface features that can be removed by adjusting the spin orientation.

Consider the scenario where $p$ lies between 1 and infinity, $
u$ ranges between 0.5 and infinity, and $\mathcal{S}_
u$ denotes the set of non-zero vectors in 2D space with a polar angle smaller than $ rac{\pi}{2
u}$. We introduce $R > 0$, and $\omega_p(x)$ as the p-harmonic measure of $\partial B(0,R) \cap \mathcal{S}_
u$ at point $x$, relative to the ball $B(0,R)\cap \mathcal{S}_
u$. We show that for some constant $C$, $\omega_p(x)$ satisfies a specific inequality with respect to the exponent $k(
u,p)$, where the exponent depends on both $
u$ and $p$, and use this estimate to derive local growth rates for certain nonlinear partial differential equations, such as those employed in the study of semiconductors and fluid dynamics, within certain highly symmetrical domains near points of high singularity.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-related geometry into a concise, actionable representation that facilitates teaching robots human-like motion through pose data and also enables emulation of human tasks from pose data. In many instances, the required manipulation ellipsoids cannot be constructed using just vision data; as a result, additional constraints from inertial sensors like IMUs must be incorporated into the process. However, existing methods in this space directly attach uncertainty to the ellipsoids without addressing the local optimality issues, which leads to suboptimal performance in local planning and motion control as a result. In light of this challenge, we introduce an approach to optimize manipulability ellipsoids along with factor graphs containing uncertainty, where the latter is learned from both pose and IMU data via a least-squares solvers that leverages a graph regularization term to obtain robust estimations. Various experiments are presented that demonstrate our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines that do not consider uncertainty.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency.

A common assumption in 3D object pose estimation involves using single-view images along with 3D object models to calculate possible poses in a canonical space. Our approach, a novel method that addresses in-the-wild single-view-three-d object pose estimation, does not require this assumption. Instead, our network directly predicts the 6-DoF pose of a real-world object from a single image. To counter data scarcity for novel object categories, we've incorporated in-the-wild video data into our approach. This type of data far exceeds the existing repositories for conventional objects, making it an ideal source for enhancing our prediction. As a result, our two-stage network first predicts the object's translation and rotation in a image-based space before transforming these into a 3D real-world coordinate system. This process also enables us to leverage in-the-wild video data containing the same object at various poses, thus providing a means to rank our network's predictions. Our extensive evaluations on multiple objects and datasets reveal that our novel approach surpasses state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we've observed that utilizing in-the-wild video data significantly enhances 3D pose estimation when compared to more conventional sources like PASCAL VOC and KITTI.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel neural framework, utilizing knowledge graphs to organize stances, successfully identifies attitudes toward this misinformation with outstanding results, outperforming other current approaches. Experiments were conducted on a newly created dataset consisting of stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation collected from online forums. This dataset is known as the COVIDStance-MIS information dataset and can be accessed freely at this link https://tinyurl.com/covidstanceMIS.

Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving two interconnected technological milestones linked to high-order harmonic generation sources. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the faintest electronic processes, while also attaining better spectral tunability would grant selectivity in targeting specific electronic transitions. Breakthroughs are made feasible by parametric waveform synthesis, giving scientists the capability to craft controllable, highly-tunable high-energy electric transients. Our findings demonstrate that by manipulating the waveform of the driving laser pulse via its relative phase and carrier-envelope phase, it's possible to exert fine-grained control over attosecond pulse characteristics. This innovation not only amplifies experimental possibilities in the realm of attosecond science, but also paves the way for a highly sophisticated, coherent manipulation of free-electron paths.

Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising older data that is no longer accurate. This involves accounting for potential companions that can create recurring periods in time shifts. A study discovered a low probability (0.00005%) of detecting new companions using eclipse time shifts. Researchers analyzed data on Algol ($\beta$ Persei) and found tentative signs of up to five additional companion candidates, which are believed to have orbital periods ranging from 1.863 to 219 years. These signals are consistent across 236 years of data and also matched the first 226.2 years of the data, accurately predicting eclipses for the following 9.2 years. The companion candidates' orbital planes are thought to be aligned due to the stable and unchanging eclipses of Algol since the early observations of Goodricke (1783).

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the existence of solutions radiating outward from a point in space and provide estimates for their maximum value, thus potentially allowing for the meromorphic extension of the associated Birkhoff function in a complex $\lambda$-space. It's also shown that the initial value problem for this equation is strictly Hamiltonian, allowing us to derive a conservation of energy quantity that includes a derivative of the solution's $L^2$ value. This new energy equation, combined with an inequality relating the solution's $L^p$ value to its maximum value, plays a key role in our collapse argument.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform sampling techniques have previously been explored, each showing benefits. To leverage these insights, we introduce Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines an adaptive algorithm for determining solution evaluation points and a non-uniform sampling method for integrating model outputs. We then evaluate this method's performance on two partial differential equations and demonstrate its efficiency and accuracy improvements compared to traditional sampling methods.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations, and find that the system converges to a stable thermodynamic state through energy minimization. Our analysis also shows that the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material leads to the negative capacitance effect, which in turn affects the device's drain current and variability due to the domain period. We also investigated how the domain wall's soft or hard state transition influences the device's electrical properties and transport. Our simulations are verified through both experimental data and phase-field modeling.

A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerability dissemination occurs within it. Existing studies that generalize security management approaches across multiple ecosystems often overlook the unique technical characteristics of individual ecosystems, hindering direct applicability of security governance strategies to Cargo. To address this disparity, this study conducts a comprehensive examination of Cargo's ecosystem, revealing crucial knowledge of its components and vulnerability dissemination paths. By utilizing a novel, ecosystem-specific security vulnerability classification taxonomy, this paper develops a statistical analysis framework to evaluate the effectiveness of Cargo's security governance. Through this framework, over 95% of Cargo ecosystem vulnerabilities were classified, and more than 20,000 vulnerabilities were linked to Cargo's ecosystem, with more than 80% caused by buffer-Related Vulnerabilities. Additionally, this paper proposes a cargo-vul-vocab vocabulary to aid in vocabulary building and provides code implementations on GitHub to facilitate further research and development. Based on the findings of 1,946 published vulnerabilities, this paper also presents various vulnerability types, owners, vulnerability fixation timelines, and other key characteristics of Cargo's ecosystem. Finally, through correlation analysis, this study identifies potential vulnerability factors and provides actionable suggestions for Cargo's ecosystem vendors and Cargo developers.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and shows these results can be extended to a broader class of stochastic equations involving multiplicative noise. Additionally, it compares the irreducibility criteria for stochastic equations with additive and multiplicative noise.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've pinpointed vertices related to its cyclic subgroups. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. This study provides degree calculations for specific types of noncyclic abelian groups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited in their ability to handle non-rigidity in images. In contrast, recent advancements in Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs) have demonstrated an unwavering performance across various challenges. However, the true potential of OCNs remains underexplored due to a lack of comprehensive analysis and substitution capabilities. To address this knowledge gap, we thoroughly evaluated multiple substitution scenarios in which different components of strong OCNs were replaced with those of weaker DCNNs. The extensive research conducted on four distinct recognition tasks within two diverse domain datasets resulted in a solid substitution benchmark, known as the Orientated Image Representation (OIR) benchmark. The OIR benchmark serves as a guide for future research, highlighting key areas for improvement and setting the standard for future comparison. To ensure the fairness and durability of the benchmark, the code, models, and custom datasets have been publicly archived at the repository address https://github.com/flashstream/oir-benchmark.

This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. Our findings indicate that the search results of multiple layers' KNN queries exhibit persistence and can be memorized, thus eliminating the need for repeated KNN searches. Furthermore, by integrating the graph convolution with the unified graph, our method achieves superior performance while significantly reducing computational costs and memory requirements. Specifically, our experiments demonstrate that the required memory for the method can be reduced by two orders of magnitude. Our optimized framework, named Efficient GCN, demonstrates superior computational efficiency and achieves comparable or better results on various datasets. Our code is available at the repository link.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as full-resolution representations of meaningful object classes. As our backdoored classifier is designed to recognize the inherent concepts of trigger images rather than specific patterns, it can be triggered by semantically similar images with distinct appearances, making our attack more applicable and resilient to countermeasures in real-world scenarios. Our experiments show that even with limited Trojan patterns and a minimal amount of poisoned data, our approach can adapt to new trigger images within the same class and evade sophisticated defense strategies effectively.

We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will allow for a spectral range of 1800 Angstroms with a resolution of 2000. Our current progress includes preparing the optics, coating the first slicer, crafting the mounts, and writing the software, all aiming to enhance IMACS's functionality by offering a more efficient way to examine extended objects and narrow-line emitters.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments.
