Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THM) measurements.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars with known volatile depletions, based on a specific stellar indicator. Our findings are presented in a table outlining mass ratio, solar metallicity, and volatile depletions for each star. Additionally, we present simulations of terrestrial exoplanet mass-radius distributions that take volatile depletions into account. Our results show significant improvements when compared to predictions based on a common default star model. These simulations also imply that future mass-radius measurements of exoplanets discovered by the BRITE constellation will yield crucial insights into planetary composition and the mass ratio of Earth-size exoplanets.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features. The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two railway environments under varying conditions, resulting in a superior performance compared to a conventional DNN.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We investigate functions defined on the vertices of the Hamming graphs H(n,q), focusing specifically on those with support contained in the direct sum of the eigenspaces U_i(n,q), U_{i+1}(n,q),..., U_j(n,q) where 0 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n. Under certain conditions, specifically when n is greater than or equal to the sum of i and j, and when the size of the alphabet is 3 or greater, we identify the functions with minimum possible support and establish a characterization for those with such a minimum. In scenarios where n is less than the sum of i and j, but with a sufficiently large alphabet size of at least 4, we identify similar properties of functions. In particular, we establish a characterization for the functions within the eigenspace U_i(n,q) with minimum possible support in several specific scenarios.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's original GUI but within an internet accessible interface, offering the same functionality as the original application. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and view tutorial and user guide information at http://shiny.copasi.org/help/.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves to be more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. In this work, a comprehensive framework built around variance components is developed for quantifying uncertainty in NNs, demonstrating its broad applicability to problems in physics and engineering where data is inherently noisy. By analyzing the underlying mathematical structures behind loss, prediction, and optimization operations within neural networks, this new framework successfully identifies and structurally quantifies three primary sources of uncertainty: noise, data deficiency, and model failure. To validate the framework's utility, comprehensive evaluations using well-documented datasets from multiple fields - including helicopter rotor noise, wind turbine aerodynamics, and heavy machinery acoustic emissions - are conducted to assess its performance against conventional metrics and standards for accuracy and reliability.

We are investigating quantum group analogues of the free group factors' radial subalgebras, specifically those of class functions, within the context of compact quantum groups and their associated radial subalgebras. We found that the class functions' radial subalgebras of $SU_q(2)$ can be broken down into two distinct $C^*$-algebras, one comprising the quantum analogues of the free group factors' quasi-split embeddings and the other comprising the quantum analogues of the maximal embeddings. Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale MPS, was considered. Inexact policy iteration includes methods such as $L_U$-inexact policy iteration where the value function update is inexact according to a locally equivalent monotone operator, and this method has a globally convergent contraction rate equivalent to that of policy iteration. Furthermore, this method and an algorithm for large-scale finite Markov decision processes, which is based on a globally convergent algorithm for monotone linearly constrained quadratic problems, have globally converging variants with locally equivalent contraction rates in a large-scale MPS. A variant of an inexact policy iteration algorithm for large-scale finite Markov decision processes, which is similar to the globally optimally efficient policy iteration algorithm, has a globally converging variant with a locally equivalent contraction rate in a large-scale MPS. A test on a large-scale finite Markov decision process, which is similar to the globally optimally efficient policy iteration algorithm, shows its efficiency compared to value function iteration.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to approximate the output, and then applying a specialized method to estimate optimal input parameters at those points, while accounting for any uncertainty in the solution. A comprehensive simulation-based study compares the proposed technique with other established methods on a variety of scenarios.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to Gourdeau et al. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robust empirical risk minimization (ERM), a robust measure of model accuracy. Our first learning model utilizes local membership queries (LMQs) to achieve robust ERM, with its ERM guarantee strengthened and its ERM loss gap analysis narrowed compared to previous research. The second learning model allows the learner to choose between label queries or LMQs, with its analysis resulting in more relaxed requirements on the data distribution assumption to guarantee the learning model's robustness. These new algorithms have lower sample complexity requirements compared to the model introduced by Gourdeau et al. (2019), with their requirements also stated in terms of the maximum concept density.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the parent parton can be well constrained. In central lead-lead collisions, variations in fragmentation functions compared to those measured in proton-proton collisions were detected, however, little deviation was seen in collisions occurring outside the main collision zone. Jets within the central zone exhibited a higher ratio of universality, undifferentiated particles to charged particles, when compared to proton-proton events. Ratios of charged particles to universality, undifferentiated particles, with decreasing transverse momentum, also showed increased suppression in lead-lead collisions. This analysis is sensitive to two distinct phases: when partons traverse the entire quark-gluon plasma or partons only pass through the quark-gluon plasma's periphery.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes for the object. New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that the object is among a select few with extremely faint proper motion, indicating it has a very low temperature consistent with the coolest Y dwarfs. Moreover, the object possesses color indices of W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 about 1.6 mag bluer than a typical Y dwarf. New data collected from WISE, Spitzer, and HST for parallax measurement have determined a close distance of $16.3^{+1.4}_{-1.2}$ parsecs and a substantial transverse velocity of $207.4{\pm}15.9$ km/s. The calculated J, W2, and ch2 absolute magnitudes align with the coolest Y dwarfs despite W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 indices displaying a distinct discrepancy. Research suggests that the object is most likely an ancient metal-poor brown dwarf and possibly the initial instance of a Y subdwarf, necessitating further examination through broad-band spectroscopy and photometry using the JWST for validation of the hypothesis.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio distributions unaffected by the system change.
Notably, our study confirms that the observed increase in radial flow with 
increasing event multiplicity is not dependent on the colliding system.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching.

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, in the form of cylinders, were created using a combination of saltwater and heat, and then fired at various temperatures to analyze their internal structure, strength and contraction. The internal structures of these materials were studied under a microscope and their mechanical properties were tested using a universal testing machine. The experiment was performed twice using different types of simulants for Martian and Lunar soil, resulting in manufactured samples resembling traditional building blocks and the initial stages of 3D printing with a binder. The results indicated that the optimal firing temperature for both types of simulants lies between 1100 C and 1200 C. The compressive strength of these materials met the requirements for building structures on other planets, suggesting their potential for use as building materials in extraterrestrial construction and as a base material for additive manufacturing processes similar to 3D printing with a binder.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations. Experimental verification of these findings is currently underway.

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST.

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. In this particular study, we classify the braided auto-equivalences of the local modules in categories linked to known type I quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. It has been determined that the symmetries exhibited in this research are all non-exceptional apart from four unique instances, which can be accounted for under the influence of level-one extended center $\mathcal{Z}^{ext}$ of the underlying moduli space $\mathcal{O}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. In the subsequent paper, we will leverage the classification achieved here to categorize a substantial number of type II quantum subgroups within $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that several of these type II subgroups possess a non-superfluid level-one extended center, enabling us to demonstrate that certain of these subgroups correspond to principles of non-superfluid center-raising operators. Such operators essentially transform different $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in similar research fields.

This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by El-Dahdah et al, focusing on classifying handwritten mathematical terms into two categories: related and unrelated. A binary classifier is proposed to accomplish this task. This classifier relies on a pre-trained convolutional neural network to generate visual feature data, which is then combined with contextual information and subject to a classification decision utilizing a support vector machine. The proposed approach demonstrates high accuracy in both mathematical term and text classification tasks. Furthermore, it is shown that by incorporating contextual words from the question, the proposed classifier's performance can be enhanced. The challenge's performance benchmarks are also surpassed with this method.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations demonstrate that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech.

Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, similar detection processes can be assumed for each species, however, this approach does not account for potential species interactions influencing detection probabilities. A new flexible model, the correlated occupancy model, has been developed to incorporate species interactions in a general framework. This model can be reduced to the standard occupancy model under specific conditions. By applying the correlated occupancy model to data from camera traps in a Yellowstone National Park ecosystem, research revealed occupation trends in elk, white-tailed deer, mule deer, and gray wolf populations. A comparative study between the correlated and standard models through leave-one-species-time analyses demonstrated that the correlated model offers a more accurate species distribution estimation, particularly for species potentially influencing detection probabilities. This study has provided essential insights into species interactions detected through occupancy analysis.

Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to artificial intelligence. The Skincare project aimed to address this by creating an innovative diagnostic and decision support system in dermatology. It combined the capabilities of interactive machine learning with deep learning to enhance the skills of doctors and augment decision-making abilities. The project's primary objective was to develop a diagnostic tool that could be utilized by dermatologists and non-dermatologists, providing these users with control to guide diagnostic processes and output feedback. This interactive deep learning system was optimized for use on low-power devices, facilitating deployment in areas with limited infrastructure and making it suitable for widespread adoption. After collecting a diverse dataset of malignant and benign skin lesions, researchers interactively trained a deep learning model, collecting data from multiple sources, including expert feedback and user interactions with the system. The project's outcomes focused on improving diagnostic accuracy for both dermatologists and non-dermatologists, with a key outcome being the development of a diagnostic tool that is accessible on low-power devices and offers a new, promising approach to support decision-making in the complex field of dermatology.

To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Normalizing Flow component after initial training using an Auto-Encoder. The model's two-stage generative architecture can identify a reduced-dimensional representation of SNe Ia, accurately modeling their spectral evolution across wavelength and time directly from data. Introducing a penalty term to address variability correlations and a multi-stage training framework within our physically-parameterized network enabled the separation of intrinsic and extrinsic variability, eliminating the need for magnitude standardization models. The PAE was applied to the complete dataset of the SN-Ia subset within the Essence archive, a dataset comprising 202 spectral time series from SNe Ia with diverse brightness levels and coverage spanning zero to two years after explosion. The PAE achieved exceptional results in both predictive and statistical tasks. The implicit probability distribution learned by the PAE was sufficiently comprehensive to effectively model irregular spectral developments in individual SNe Ia, even those not included in the initial training set. Furthermore, the PAE's latent space consistently grouped SNe Ia by velocity without any prior knowledge of the explosions' characteristics. The PAE's reconstruction errors demonstrated a relationship with brightness, with broader variability ranges observed in the brighter portion of the sample. This research presents a novel approach to using probabilistic autoencoders for supernovae data and offers a framework for applying such models within highly dynamic and complex astronomical systems.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a gravitationally lensed star-forming galaxy. The outflow is visible in a specific OH+ absorption line, which was measured by the ALMA telescope at high spatial resolution. The data also include CO emission, dust, and stellar light. Analysis of the outflow shows that it has different properties than other elements within the galaxy. The mass of the outflow is estimated to be approximately 6.7 billion solar masses. The outflow's properties are best explained by a conical shape. Depending on the inclination angle, the outflow's rate of gas loss and kinetic energy could be quite high. This suggests that the outflow may impact the galaxy's star formation. The outflow may eventually be re-accreted back into the galaxy, but this would depend on various feedback mechanisms. The estimated gas depletion time in the galaxy is around 1-29 million years.

To study the movement of fluid into a swirling, turbulent plume containing heavy particles that sink more slowly than the plume moves, researchers used controlled experiments in a lab setting. The experiments focused on the effects of particle size, density, and the direction in which the plume gains mass, as well as the direction in which the particles move within the plume. The studies showed that when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, the movement of fluid into the plume increases significantly. The rate of fluid movement increased in direct proportion to the ratio of the particles' gain of mass to the fluid's gain of mass, and this increased rate was independent of particle size. In contrast, when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are the same, adding particles has no effect on fluid movement. The observed increase in fluid movement, which occurs when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, can be attributed to inertial clustering, a phenomenon where particles move along the outer layers of swirling flows. The increased movement of fluid into the plume can then be understood as a result of the increased velocity of these outer layers and the decreased diameter of the plume. The observed effect, which varies based on the direction in which the plume gains mass, can be understood as a result of the balance between two forces, one that slows

Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the number of infectious contacts a person has. This approach leads us to develop new spectral conditions and study various types of contagion models, considering both the stochastic individual-level model and the mean-field approximation. Numerical examples and the analysis that follows enable the differentiation between inherent disease characteristics and the impact of individual actions. Ultimately, this framework holds potential for a more precise evaluation of the effectiveness of virus containment interventions.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an in-plane magnetization orientation. Their investigation reveals that this ferromagnetic bilayer displays a rich pattern of spin texture within its uppermost valence bands, which arises from two unique spin cants resulting from the interplay of ferromagnetic order with both chirality and electrical polarization. One type of cant is a result of layer stacking asymmetry and valence state polarization, resulting in equivalent canting patterns on both layers. Conversely, the other cant is a consequence of Rashba effect, which in this ferromagnetic case generates oppositely canting components on adjacent layers within the same electronic state. Additionally, researchers formulated a set of rules governing spin polarization behavior within magnetic crystals based on their magnetic symmetry properties. Lastly, they found that applying compressive strain could effectively control the shape of spin texture within ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayers by creating valence-band states with spins that can be aligned.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of the magnetic fields responsible for the stellar activity decline observed in the solar twin approach. To thoroughly understand stellar activity, it's essential to comprehend the link between rotation frequency and coronal emission through the entire solar life cycle and beyond.

Deep multimodal learning using K-fan deep Boltzmann machines offers a novel approach to combine multiple input sources. This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine models lies in their inability to handle complex tasks effectively, particularly when multiple input modalities are incomplete or missing. We present a K-fan deep model, featuring a K-branch architecture for handling multi-input, multi-output tasks efficiently. Each branch of the model can comprise multiple layers of neural networks. A shared representation is learned in a discriminative manner to tackle multiple tasks. Models with multiple-fan structures, such as two-fan and three-fan Deep Boltzmann machine models, are also developed as specialized cases of the proposed K-fan deep model. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on various multimedia classification datasets, demonstrating its superiority over existing approaches.

The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to the hidden nature of race conditions, which can evade detection by these tests. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The effectiveness of McMini's use in detecting race conditions has been demonstrated in two independent studies one involving a multi-user database application and the other a multi-threaded media player program both of which yielded positive results after applying model checking.

The globally predominant messaging app, WhatsApp, boasts a distinct characteristic 
in its closed nature and user-friendly capabilities of transferring multimedia and
large-scale information sharing to groups, which often facilitates the rapid spread 
of anonymous, encrypted messages. However, the direct delivery of messages to user 
phones enabled by WhatsApp, although personal and immediate, can be exploited to 
circulate baseless rumors and fuel misinformation campaigns. Recent elections in 
Brazil and India are notable examples of such abuse, which have led WhatsApp to 
initiate countermeasures like limiting forwarded messages to a single recipient. 
Despite this effort, the success of these measures remains uncertain. In our study, 
we utilize an epidemiological model coupled with real data from WhatsApp in Brazil, 
India, and Indonesia to investigate the impact of limiting features that contribute 
to rapid information dissemination. Our analysis reveals that current WhatsApp 
restrictions can delay the spread of information but are ultimately insufficient to 
halt the dissemination of highly viral misinformation campaigns within public groups.

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model. This model treats state changes in the population as a result of either one of two events: either a mutating event that causes population growth at a specified rate, or a non-mutating event occurring at a different rate. This two-event scenario leads to a characterization of the population's frequency spectrum through a specific non-negative matrix. This characterization enables us to derive conditions under which the population's frequency spectrum becomes uniformly distributed on the interval $[0,1]$. Additionally, by applying the Descartes' rule of signs, we establish the criteria for the population's frequency spectrum to have either all positive or all negative values. Moreover, we use the characteristics of the frequency spectrum to derive various inequalities involving key parameters of the population, including the average frequency, the relative standard deviation of the frequency, and the spectral standardization of the frequency. These inequalities can be seen as particular cases of two established inequalities in the literature, thereby validating previously published results and extending them in significant ways.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access dataset, an acoustic dataset previously utilized in various studies, but notably absent from the existing literature. Following extensive training and feature extraction processes, a comprehensive model was constructed using the extracted features as input, subsequently subjected to multiple model iterations, including the effective utilization of hard attention, soft attention, and weighted average pooling methods. Our final model was validated on the logical access dataset, yielding a notable 16% improvement in the accuracy of our spoofing detection model.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding. Despite this potential, constructing self-consistent inflationary models within supergravity is a significant challenge due to the presence of $R$-symmetry and Goldstone modes that complicate the dynamics. These new degrees of freedom can give rise to unwanted entropy during the inflationary period, creating problems for model building. However, we argue that these new degrees of freedom can be utilized to create highly entropy-dense particles during inflation, leading to distinct predictions in early Universe observations. By examining hypothetical inflationary models, we illustrate how $R$-symmetry and Goldstone modes can give rise to these particle creation processes, which tend to occur at frequencies comparable to or higher than the inflationary scale. This particle creation process can be impeded or facilitated according to the underlying model's characteristics. Consequently, the likelihood of detecting these particles in future cosmic experiments should be considered a viable possibility.

Nonreciprocal optical systems are highly functional in various applications but
induce identical effects for concurrent and opposite directions of signal
propagation. We propose an innovative design of a nonreciprocal optical metasurface
that modulates the phase of light via the nonlinear response of second-order
magnetoelectric effects in magnon-polaritons. When studied under the conditions
of spontaneous four-wave mixing, it demonstrates a significant variation in the
correlated photon pair's frequency dependence on the direction of the signal's 
propagation. Additionally, while classical nonlinear elements fail to produce a
similar impact, the presented device exhibits an elevated conversion efficiency in
comparison to previous research involving nonreciprocal optical systems, thus 
manifesting a crucial distinction in photon pair correlations.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices.

We are looking for infinite cardinals $\kappa$ that allow for a division of the real number line $\mathbb R$ into $\kappa$ unique Borel sets. The well-known Hausdorff solution indicates that $\aleph_1$ sets work in one instance. Our research shows that the size range for these divisions can vary extensively, allowing any uncountable regular cardinal $\kappa$ to be included. The proof method involves showing that if $\mathbb R$ can be partitioned into $\kappa$ Borel sets, then a specific homogeneous space $\kappa\times\mathbb R$ can also be divided into $\kappa$ consistent Borel sets.

In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - in markets with both types of traders, CTA profitability and activity actually increased. Consequently, a positive symbiotic relationship between these traders may be more likely than initially assumed.

Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed inspection. Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, solely relying on static characteristics like port numbers can be insufficient. As a result, advanced and adaptive approaches have been developed for more precise identification. In this research, the mechanisms of dynamic protocol detection in widely used open-source network monitoring tools are examined, with a focus on Suricata. Our in-depth analysis dissects each component that contributes to detecting application protocols in Suricata and highlights the impact of real-time network traffic on this process. To compare the performance of different methods, our study leverages a comprehensive traffic dataset and evaluates various metrics, including accuracy, threshold scores, false positives, and training efficiency. Ultimately, our investigation suggests that manually configuring Suricata's profile based on expert knowledge can yield improved results and threshold efficiency when compared to other methods.

Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance to stray magnetic fields. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this response effectively halt the forward flow of magnons perpendicular to the magnetic field. By positioning two superconducting gates in parallel with the magnetic field, we were able to create a confined magnon system. The added capability to control coherent magnons enables new functionalities in magnonic devices, including reconfigurable logical circuits and stronger connections to other systems of degrees of freedom.

A beneficial approach for enhancing user equity and keeping user data private exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, the possibility of data bias rising due to non-uniform data distribution across users impedes the development process. To tackle this challenge, we design and test an innovative federated learning framework that incorporates both federated averaging and differential privacy techniques. The novel approach involves a data bias correction process that utilizes Poisson distribution to balance the data distribution and a bias-corrected aggregation point. This method serves as a more transparent alternative to using synthetic data to mitigate bias, and it significantly outperforms such methods in terms of model performance. Notably, our approach offers a reliable solution to the previously-cited issue, thereby contributing to and expanding upon existing research in this domain. The proposed framework also addresses the question of whether synthetic data can be an effective means to the ends. The developed approach is put through testing in the context of BRCA1 and BRCA2 genetic data annotation, and the results indicate its severe impacts on model performance when synthetic data is used with bias correction methods. Conversely, the novel approach demonstrates improved accuracy when handling non-IID data scenarios. The success of this method also relies on several key parameters, including the data distribution parameters within users' datasets, and the number of users participating in the learning process.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both hyperentanglement of photons and the quantum Fourier transform are employed. The proposed solution will serve as a useful resource for developing high-dimensional quantum computation and communication.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink cascaded channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems aided by intelligent-reflecting-surfaces operating within the sub-6 GHz frequency range where channel propagation isn't sparse. A high-performance, low-overhead estimation protocol has been developed to minimize reflection power loss without requiring on-off amplitude control. The proposed solution exploits a common structure within the system, significantly reducing pilot transmission overhead by decomposing the complex cascaded channel into separate user-specific and shared variables. The challenge of highly coupled estimation variables is overcome through the use of optimization-based estimation methods utilizing channel covariance. An alternating optimization algorithm has been developed to efficiently solve the resulting non-convex problem, with an efficient initialization technique ensuring a local optimal solution. The research further introduces a successive convex approximation algorithm for optimizing the protocol's training phase, leading to improved accuracy. The authors conduct comprehensive simulations, which show that the proposed algorithm yields superior performance relative to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information.

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In the realm of machine learning, this capability seems to be equally essential for humans in guiding robotic tasks. To uncover the underlying logic of this process, we conducted a detailed analysis of a teacher's guidance provided through verbal counting cues during a robotic arm's learning process. Our research demonstrates that the model we developed can effectively capture the essence of this guidance by pinpointing key phases or inflection points in the learning process. Our findings also emphasize the importance of initial guidance and highlight potential drawbacks of delayed or insufficient teaching. Moreover, we speculate that our model can serve as a more sophisticated tool for robot teaching, allowing for more efficient and effective instruction.

Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter. A modification to this concept has also been explored, particularly by Dietzfelbinger and Pagh. Their variation of the Bloomier filter can serve approximate membership queries efficiently, though no comprehensive testing of it exists to date. A different filter was developed, the xor filter, as an implementation of their idea, offering more effective efficiency and speeds. Notably, the developed xor filter can surpass both Bloom and cuckoo filters in performance, all while consuming even less storage space than these solutions. A proposed variant of the Bloomier filter can also provide several times the performance improvement of its competitors, even when needing only a single storage unit to function correctly.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively.

A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to optimal values, thereby maximizing trading volume per unit of time. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. To facilitate trend analysis, both historical and forecasted price data are considered, with past prices represented by lagging values and forecasted prices represented by advancing values.

This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and precludes data exposure from the server.

We successfully submitted the winning entry to the NeurIPS 2021 - AWS Deepracer challenge, which required developing a self-driving vehicle model that interacts with its environment through reaction and reward feedback. The competition evaluated the models' ability to navigate a simulated track, complete a lap at high speed, and respond to various on-track situations in a real-world setting. Our approach to solving this task involved creating a reinforcement learning model with a novel policy network architecture, which utilized a sparse, customized reward scheme to optimize learning efficiency. Additionally, we designed a dynamic sensor model to reduce the computational requirements for training and improved the model's performance through a dataset augmentation technique that utilized virtual vehicles to enhance learning from existing data.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter examines the advancements and difficulties in the production and identification of deepfakes, and also explores the potential solutions to improve the resilience of deepfake detection for a broad range of media, such as real-world images and videos. Furthermore, it proposes future research directions for tackling deepfake-related issues.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement for a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being a non-equilibrium condition in massive atmospheres. Notably, the reduced carbon dioxide levels and higher temperatures in massive atmospheres would restrict photochemical nitrogen gas production, ultimately leading to distinct clines among sub-Neptune exoplanets in the mass-habitable space, effectively limiting the mass range in which sub-Neptune exoplanets can support liquid water oceans and potentially support life.

Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns of binary vectors, an ability similar to that of symmetric Hopfield networks for spatial patterns. Furthermore, our study reveals the model's capability to efficiently acquire sequences of binary images and generate neural spike-train data. Our model adheres to spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) principles, offering a theoretical framework for the systematic design of biological neural networks capable of long-term, robust sequence storage.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis presented encompasses a thorough evaluation of various training techniques and their effects on holistically recognizing unique text instances.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent systems and generalizes seamlessly to multi-parameter tracking. To demonstrate the proposed methodology, this research achieves the precise calculation of random equilibrium cycles in the Lorenz system, as well as solution branches and 2-dimensional planes of steady states in the Swift-Hohenberg equation.

The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and available resources. Moreover, industrial systems may exhibit multiple failure patterns, and identifying the primary cause is essential. This work aims to develop an adaptive monitoring system capable of handling high-dimensional data in resource-scarce environments where various potential failures may occur. By integrating a statistical method with a model-free approach, the proposed framework utilizes a Gaussian Mixture Model to identify anomalies and perform failure mode isolation, thus enhancing overall diagnostic efficiency and accuracy. Evaluations using public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the adaptive monitoring system, revealing superior performance compared to established methods.

We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that merged with the Milky Way's outer layers: the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 (WLM) galaxies. Our sophisticated computational model, designed to simulate galaxy growth patterns, is based on exponential infall scenarios and aligns with contemporary knowledge of galaxy evolution. By matching key features with observed data, we adjusted the model's parameters and calculated various timescales for each galaxy. The results indicate that both GSE and WLM experienced rapid infall phases in the early stages, with infalling material initially avoiding the center and accumulating at distances of 5-20 kpc over multiple Gyr. Notably, our analysis indicates that WLM began forming stars earlier (around 10 billion years ago) with a magnetic wheelbarrow shape, featuring a bulge and distinct spiral arms, and consisting of two dominant gas components: a large, rotating disk and a central gas structure. Our results also indicate a late, rapid growth phase (around 8-9 billion years ago) in both galaxies, suggesting a possible merger event that contributed to their eventual absorption by the Milky Way. Our findings are consistent with observed features and are presented in an easily interpretable format, and we anticipate that our results will facilitate further research into the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus and Wukong/LMS-1 galaxies.

Given a profinite group G, an S[[G]]-module is a G-spectrum that fulfills certain criteria, leading to the definition of the homotopy orbit spectrum X_{hG} associated with an S[[G]]-module X. When X's constituents meet specific finiteness criteria, a homotopy orbit spectral sequence arises with an E2-term being the continuous homology of G, taking coefficients from the graded profinite \widehat{\mathbb{Z}}[[G]]-module \pi_*(X). This is demonstrated with an equivalence for certain conditions on G and Z: specifically, (Z[[G]])_{hG} is shown to be equivalent to Z in those scenarios, with supplementary methods for further investigation provided.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices. Using a computational model that incorporates machine-learned data and density functional theory, we have studied how varying the bonding configuration at the interface impacts the electronic properties. Across the examined configurations, we observed that the energy levels at the interface in InAs are positioned higher than those in EuS. Furthermore, we discovered novel states that arise from the interaction between the two materials, and are localized at the interface due to charge transfer. The arrangement of atoms at the interface significantly influences both the energy position and distribution of these states. While an induced magnetic effect is evident in InAs, the magnetic moment is relatively weak.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively decreasing training costs. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, efficiently and accurately enables both end-to-end training and model pruning for CNNs, distinguishing itself from previous work with fine-grained architecture preservation through pattern-based pruning, precise weight estimation, and compiler-optimized calculations. As a result, ClickTrain can deploy high-accuracy and fast-pruned models directly without additional overhead compared to traditional methods, while also minimizing the pruning-after-training approach by 2.3 times with similar results and reducing the training time for equal accuracy by 2.6 times with over 16% higher accuracy performance.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by introducing modal operators to various substructures within these logics. The study specifically focuses on three specific substructures - canonical extensions, free bounded distributive lattice extensions, and lattice ordered groups. The underlying goal is to understand how these substructures impact the corresponding modal logics and their deductive systems.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Existing approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel deep learning architectures based on Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks that significantly enhance the accuracy of signal recovery for all types of compact binary mergers in numerical simulations. These models also demonstrate the capability to classify events at an impressive 97.6% accuracy for low signal-to-noise ratios and 99.9% for high signal-to-noise ratios. With its exceptional performance, this method sets the foundation for a pioneering solution in real-time gravitational wave detection and classification within future observational projects.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 approximately every 75 days. Initially detected by the TESS satellite, the exoplanet, which has a radius similar to that of Jupiter, has been confirmed through multiple follow-up analyses using ground-based observatories. Analysis of this new finding, combined with data on the host star, which is approximately 10 billion years old and made up of metal-rich elements, suggests that TOI-5542b is likely a giant planet. Research suggests that this new discovery is part of a newly detected class of small, cool giant planets. Data from future observations with the JWST and Hanumanian satellites indicate that the exoplanet's temperature is most likely similar to that of Jupiter, given its proximity to 0.6 AU. The findings from this study, which were based on a combination of data from several sources, including radial velocity observations from NOT, which indicated a slightly varying orbital inclination throughout the data set, suggest that the exoplanet's orbit is slightly tilted relative to its orbit around the host star. The new data provide evidence suggesting that the exoplanet, TOI-5542b, is likely in a stable orbital pattern. The findings from this study have been combined to create a new analysis, which indicates that the exoplanet's mass is most likely between 0.85 and 1.3 Earth masses. The new data provide a

Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by a large number of states and actions, as well as a multitude of potential paths with uncertain outcomes. These challenges make it impractical to apply traditional methods for solving CMDPs, leading to a need for alternative approaches. Building on techniques from machine learning and probability, we have developed a new approach that approximates optimal policies for CMDPs by focusing on the identification of critical state-action pairs. To determine which pairs are significant, we utilize a neural network-based operator that scores the importance of each state-action combination based on their long-term value. We have shown that our approach can efficiently identify the most relevant state-action pairs and provide a strategy with high value, even in situations where the CMDP dynamics are partially unknown. These findings have been confirmed through numerical testing, as well as analysis of a real-world problem in operational management.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many complex mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be split, but certain symbols, like the square root symbol, can't be processed this way. What's more, handwritten mathematical symbols can look very similar, for example, handwritten zero and the Greek letter null. Given the numerous mathematical symbols, over 300 in total, a highly effective classifier capable of recognizing such a wide range of symbols must be developed. Initially, this study addressed the challenge of segmentation by applying the Simple Linear Iterative Clustering method. Results showed that the accuracy of the designed kNN classifier was 84% for the salient features, while 57% and 53% accuracies were achieved with the Histogram of Oriented Gradient (HOG) and Linear Binary Pattern (LBP) methods respectively for the salient features. Also, pixel intensity had an accuracy of 43% for the 66 classes considered. The use of the modified LeNet architecture achieved an accuracy of 90% for 87 classes and the SqueezeNet architecture reached an accuracy of  for 101 classes.

A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone that has a symplectic resolution with equivariant symplectic properties. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes on the resolved space. The classes are divided into distinct twisted Dolbeault cohomology groups, which are generated by projections of original states through a quiver construction. The weights and charges of these BPS states are determined by the equivariant properties of the resolution. The BPS state enumerative invariants can be calculated as the sums of products of twisted Gromov-Witten invariants of the hyper-Kahler cone. The invariants are further modified by factors representing the properties of stabilizers in the action of the SL(2,${\mathbb C}$) symmetry group. The relevant ingredients of the Gromov-Witten invariants are encoded in a specific comb format that corresponds to the branching patterns of weighted, irreducible, semi-simple sl(2,{${\mathbb C}$}) representations. The weights of these representations are determined by the equivariant properties of the symplectic resolution. The extreme BPS states correspond to cohomology classes on the cone, while the intermediate BPS states correspond to twisted Dolbeault cohomology classes on the resolved space. A degeneration construction is provided to show the isomorphism of the invariants and the twisted invariants for arbitrary degree and equivariance properties

We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Initially, our research reveals that the disparity in epidemic behavior between homogeneous and heterogeneous networks is surprisingly small, yet the latter's complex structure can lead to a lower overall infection rate. Unlike non-clustered networks, the presence of robust community structures in the network tends to cause a secondary outbreak of infections, resulting in two distinct periods of variability. Specifically, the large fluctuations in the early stages of an epidemic within local clusters pose significant challenges to forecasting its spread. Crucially, our analysis suggests that bridging elements within the network have a substantial impact on predictability, with increased distances from the initial infection source to these nodes corresponding to decreased accuracy in forecasting the epidemic's progression. Furthermore, our research investigates how different disease response mechanisms influence variability, revealing that diverse reaction mechanisms can yield disparate infection rates at the conclusion of an epidemic.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic model. To address this challenge, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the Hamiltonian Policy. In doing so, our novel method has yielded substantial improvements in policy quality according to both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations conducted on a variety of critical benchmark tests. Furthermore, when applied to real-world robotic scenarios, the Hamiltonian Policy has demonstrated a notable 10% improvement in success rates and up to a 30% acceleration in training process speed.

It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will refer to the number $k$ that produces a given prime $p$ as the $\textbf{generator}$ of that prime. Pairs of twin primes have the unique characteristic of sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. As a result, searching for these twin primes at the level of their respective generators makes practical sense. This paper introduces a novel strategy for verifying the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ by utilizing a sieving approach to extract all twin primes at their corresponding generator levels. In the context of $\omega_{p_n}$-numbers, $x$, we are referring to numbers that satisfy the condition that $6x-1$ and $6x+1$ are relatively prime to the prime $p_n$. We can demonstrate the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ by utilizing an infinite series of $\omega_{p_n}$-numbers, analyzing their behavior as $n$ approaches infinity, and showing that the ratio of twin primes to prime numbers approaches $2$. This realization offers a novel, groundbreaking, and highly influential strategy for understanding the distribution of prime numbers.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an intriguing spectral profile that necessitates further investigation. Our primary objective is to provide essential data for Nereid's spectral analysis, specifically its taxonomic type, by evaluating the feasibility of various solid and icy materials in relation to its reflectance spectrum. Our study indicates that Nereid cannot be categorized as a traditional asteroid type, as its spectrum does not align with any asteroid taxonomic group, particularly those featuring neutral or oxidized compositions. Conversely, Nereid's spectrum shares similarities with those of celestial bodies possessing neutral-sloped or red-sloped spectral characteristics. Our analysis also demonstrates that Na$_2$O$_2$ is a crucial component in understanding the spectral behavior of a range of icy materials. Ultimately, Nereid's spectrum appears to be better explained by considering aqueous altitudes of palagonite and/or other palagonitic materials in combination with water-ice, as these components in various proportions successfully replicate the observed spectral features, a result consistent with the hypothesis that these materials are among the outer Saturnian and Uranian systmes' spectral variants.

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its counterpart ${^2R}_n(q)$. Studies have proven that over the projective line based on $T(n, q)$, with $T(n, q)$ defined as the projective version of $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$, the free module $V_{2n}(q)$ has points in its spectrum that correspond to non-cyclic submodules. This has given rise to an interest in calculating the number of points in the spectrum of $V_{2n}(q)$. By establishing a one-to-one correspondence between the non-cyclic non-free cyclic submodules of $V_{2n}(q)$ and the affine planes of order $q$, with $n$ representing the dimension, it is now possible to determine the number of points in the spectrum of $V_{2n}(q)$. This has been found to be equivalent to $1 + \sum_{d=1}^{n-1} (q-1)q^{2d-1}$. This research further develops a one-to-one correspondence between the cyclic irreducible submodules of $V_{2n}(q)$ and the extended affine

In a 1986 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain model properties can be inferred within extensions of those models. This is proven through a novel application of Tukey-order with models, expanding upon an existing concept introduced by Vojtáš in 1991. By leveraging this notion, it can be shown that certain model properties can imply each other, thereby establishing key theorems related to random and Cohen reals within specific set-theoretic models.

A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with minimal state coverage and compensates for model uncertainty through conditional empirical distribution estimations. Mathematics show the pessimism operator is a convex operator and converges to a unique solution. The results of our study along with a policy validation method are demonstrated in two practical scenarios: treating HIV/AIDS and managing dual-eligible beneficiaries and the health care needs of individuals with mental and physical co-conditions.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship to Wakamatsu tilting bimodules, with specific cases yielding known dualities. When restricting these relationships to subcategories of finitely generated modules with particular dimensions, previously established correspondences and dualities on tilting modules are reaffirmed. The implications of this relationship include demonstrating equivalences of derived categories of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective modules, as well as the invariance of certain algebraic invariants under tilting transformations.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs many comparisons to the Witting configuration's attributes.

In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. To study this system, we develop a theory describing the interaction between magnons and Cooper pairs in flat band superconductors. Our results show that within a highly repulsive Hubbard model on an arbitrary lattice, a stable flat band superconductor emerges, exhibiting intrinsic Cooper pair spin-splitting and Majorana zero modes at corners due to chiral symmetry.
